analysis.one_liner: Sets national rules requiring companies to get consent before collecting personal data and lets people access, correct, or delete it.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Commerce Committee with no cosponsors and no vote, and a federal privacy law never passed during this Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created the first comprehensive federal consumer privacy law. Companies would need consent before collecting personal data, with stricter express consent for sensitive data like health, location, and biometric information. People would get rights to see, correct, and delete their data, and the Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general could enforce the rules with civil penalties per person affected. At the same time, the bill would have overridden state privacy laws, blocked individuals from suing companies themselves, and exempted small businesses from some rights.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people, who would gain a nationwide right to know what data companies hold, get it corrected or deleted, and stop collection they never agreed to. Sensitive data like health records, precise location, biometrics, and religious affiliation would require express affirmative consent before collection, and companies would have to run real data security programs.

how_it_helps.text: Businesses could not collect or process personal data without the individual's consent, except for limited purposes like completing a transaction, complying with law, preventing fraud, or internal operations [S2][S3].

Sensitive personal data — including health information, precise geolocation, biometric identifiers, and religious affiliation — would require express affirmative consent that cannot be inferred from inaction [S3].
Individuals could access their data in a portable format, dispute inaccuracies, and request deletion, free of charge at least twice a year [S3].
Every covered entity would have to publish a plain-language privacy policy and maintain a comprehensive data security program scaled to its size and the sensitivity of the data [S2][S3].
The FTC could impose civil penalties of up to $42,530 per affected individual for knowing violations, and the bill would direct the FTC to hire at least 440 additional enforcement staff [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Companies that profit from collecting and processing personal data, including online advertisers and data brokers, would bear compliance costs, smaller customer databases, and potential penalties. Small businesses (under 500 employees, under $50 million in gross receipts, and under data-volume thresholds) would be exempt from the access and correction rights but still subject to consent and security rules.

drawbacks.text: The bill expressly preempts state privacy laws, meaning stronger state rules — such as California's — would be overridden in favor of a single federal floor, and it strips the FCC of authority over how common carriers handle personal data [S3].
There is no private right of action: individuals could not sue companies that violate their privacy; only the FTC and state attorneys general could enforce the law [S3].

For ordinary (non-sensitive) data, silence counts as consent — companies could keep collecting unless a person affirmatively opts out, and businesses can decline requests that conflict with their 'legitimate interests' [S3].
Small businesses are exempt from the rights to access and correct data, and employee data and 'publicly available information' are excluded from the definition of personal data entirely [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A national privacy floor with real rights, security requirements, and meaningful per-person penalties would be a genuine gain for consumers. But the bill is business-shaped: it overrides stronger state laws, closes the courthouse door to individual lawsuits, defaults to opt-out consent for most data, and excludes employee and 'publicly available' information. Whether it helps or hurts consumers in practice would depend heavily on how aggressively the FTC enforced it.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, never got a single cosponsor, and sat there until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Jerry Moran introduced the bill on April 29, 2021, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation [S1][S5].
No senator signed on as a cosponsor at any point [S4].
The committee never held a markup or vote, and the bill received no further action of any kind after referral [S5].
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, killing the bill; no comprehensive federal privacy law was enacted during that Congress [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that collect and monetize personal data are better off, since the pre-2021 patchwork — no comprehensive federal privacy law and stronger rules only in a few states — remained in place. Consumers gained nothing from the bill's death, though state privacy laws were never overridden either.

for.name: Sen. Jerry Moran
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Consumer Data Privacy and Security Act of 2021 and referred it to the Commerce Committee

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Maria Cantwell (D-WA)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a markup or vote; the record shows no committee action after the April 2021 referral

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote and drew zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan pattern on the merits ever became visible.

industries.note: Consent and deletion requirements would shrink the data they can collect and monetize, but federal preemption and the ban on private lawsuits would shield them from stronger state rules and from being sued by individuals [S3].

industries.industry: Large online platforms and app makers
industries.note: They would face express-consent, privacy-officer, and impact-assessment duties for data on over 20 million people, but gain one uniform national rule instead of 50 state regimes [S3].

industries.industry: Banks, insurers, and HIPAA-covered health entities
industries.note: Entities already compliant with Gramm-Leach-Bliley, FCRA, or HIPAA would be deemed compliant with the new law for that data, keeping their existing regime intact [S3].

industries.industry: State governments and state attorneys general
industries.note: State AGs would gain power to sue violators and share civil penalties, but the bill would occupy the field and strike down state privacy statutes, including consumer access and deletion rights [S3].
